newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: WEEK AHEAD-S.AFRICA FEB PPI SEEN NEARING YR'S PEAK.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD-S.AFRICA FEB PPI SEEN NEARING YR'S PEAK.

text.p: Continued upward pressure on food prices, heavily-weighted survey items and the ongoing impact of the rand's fall should see producer inflation in February approaching the year's peak.
But economists were divided on the effects of a stronger currency in January on the imported component of the index -- which makes up roughly 20 percent of the total figure.

Some anticipated the imported component, which has been under pressure due to the rand's sharp decline last year, to remain roughly flat or even decline in February due to a recovery in the rand this year and sharp fall in oil prices.
But others believed the impact of the appreciating rand would only filter through around three to four months down the line.
The Producer Price Index (PPI) -- due for release on Thursday at 0900 GMT -- is seen rising 0.7 percent month-on-month or 9.5 percent year-on-year.
This compares to a 0.8 percent month-on-month and 9.2 percent rise in January.

"Imported inflation should be roughly flat or even down due to the appreciating rand in January and the sharply lower rand/oil price," said Herman van Papendorp of SMK Securities -- a view echoed by Standard Bank's economics unit.
But both Econometrix economist Tony Twine and ING Baring's Hania Farhan felt the impact of the stronger rand would be reflected only in coming months.

"Most people would have been importing goods for sale in February a couple of months back... but we will definitely see the impact of the stronger rand coming through in the coming few months in terms of lower imported prices," said Farhan.
According to Twine, the figure could already be lifted in March by the rand's better performance in January.
The unit strengthened from a worst level of 4.70 on the U.S. dollar to a best level of 4.55 during January after losing more than a fifth of its value on a trade-weighted basis in 1996.
The eight economists polled were unanimous in their views that producer inflation would peak close to 10 percent in around April or even a little later, towards mid-year.

According to Farhan, the impact of the stronger rand in terms of lower imported costs combined with technical factors should see a lower second half PPI figure, nearing 8.4 to 8.2 percent at the end of the year.

On the local side, pressure was expected from a number of heavily weighted surveys such as machinery and transport equipment (with a weighting of 17 percent) and metals and metal products (8.6 percent). This was in addition to upward pressure expected from food prices.
